newsitem.title: USA: US traders skeptical of O'Leary plan for heat oil.
newsitem.headline: US traders skeptical of O'Leary plan for heat oil.

text.p: Oil traders reacted with skepticism to suggestions made Tuesday by Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary that high U.S. heating oil prices might be curbed by luring additional imports from Venezuela.

O'Leary, expressing concern heating oil prices could spike this winter, told reporters an Energy Department official en route to Venezuela on an unrelated matter "will raise the issue of are there extra barrels to come from Venezuela."

Venezuela last year shipped an average of 58,000 barrels per day (bpd) of heating oil and diesel fuel to the United States, with similar volumes arriving from Canada and the Virgin Islands, according to Department of Energy data.

But U.S. traders said Venezuela, which has 1.2 million-barrels-per-day (bpd) of crude refining capacity, was unlikely to ship extra heating oil to the United States unless it fetched top dollar for every barrel.

"Venezuela is...already at maximum capacity because they have to pay huge international debts," said one East Coast trader with frequent dealings with Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), Venezuela's state oil company.
He said Europe and South America are as short or shorter on heating oil stocks than the United States and are also competing for Venezuelan imports.
"Venezuela is in a position to demand the highest price so why would they want to subsidize (U.S.) East Coast consumers?" the trader said.
He dismissed O'Leary's suggestion as "a fine public relations gesture" during a presidential election year.
"Most of the oil and products that we produce are under contract. That is our way of doing business," said a source with PDVSA in Caracas, who pegged its distillate production at about 440,000 bpd.
Traders noted that Venezuela ships large amounts of high- sulfur diesel fuel to Brazil and Argentina that it could conceivably divert to the United States for use as heating oil.
"But why would they divert diesel to the United States as inexpensive heating oil when they could get better dollars selling it to South America as motor oil?," one broker said

Another trader said it was ironic that Gulf Coast refiners continue to export heating oil to South America even as the U.S. government sends diplomats to Venezuela inquiring about the possibility of attracting more of their imports.
"O'Leary's idea doesn't make sense unless you want a bidding war," the trader said, adding other needy countries would bid up the ante every step of the way.
U.S. heating oil stocks are at their lowest point since the early 1970's for this time of year, according to the American Petroleum Institute (API).
Its latest inventory report, for the week ending Sept 27, estimated total U.S. stocks down 27 percent from 1995 levels.

Ron Planting, an API statistician, said monthly imports of Venezuelan heating oil often fluctuate during winter -- particularly if very cold weather or U.S. refinery problems cause heavy drawdowns in inventory.
He noted that U.S. imports of the Venezuelan fuel surged to 130,000 bpd in January 1995, but noted consumers may have had to pay extra for the additional barrels.
"The way the market works, wherever it can be sold at the highest price, that's where it will go."
